title: One drumbeat, two long crescendos
question: How does the chosen pulse change the climb from solo flute to the final brass and percussion?
intro: A snare drum starts its two-bar pattern, and a flute begins the tune of Boléro. In 1930 Ravel recorded the long crescendo with the Lamoureux Orchestra; Fricsay conducts the Berlin orchestra in the second performance. The flute’s quiet entrance has a long way to travel before the trombones and percussion bring everything down.

recordings.label: Maurice Ravel, Lamoureux Orchestra, 1930
recordings.note: The composer conducts the Lamoureux Orchestra for Polydor in January 1930.

recordings.label: Ferenc Fricsay, Berlin Symphonic Orchestra
recordings.note: Fricsay conducts Berlin’s orchestra in a recording restored by Pablo Varela in 2015.

passages.label: The flute begins
passages.note: A solo flute curls through the first tune above the snare drum and plucked strings. The bass alternates C and G.

passages.label: The oboe d’amore’s turn
passages.note: The oboe d’amore brings back the first melody. Bassoons take up the drum’s rhythm while the strings keep plucking.

passages.label: Horn, celesta and two piccolos
passages.note: A horn carries the tune beneath celesta and two piccolos. Their notes at different heights combine into one strange, bright voice.

passages.label: Eight bars in E major
passages.note: The bass finally leaves C, and the orchestra swings into E major. The drum’s two-bar rhythm carries on through the sudden change.

passages.label: Trombone slides and the final crash
passages.note: C major returns with trombone slides. Bass drum, cymbals and tam-tam join the last six bars, and the orchestra brings the dance crashing to a halt.
